evals.prompt: A user says 'this Rust function is slow, make it fast' with no profile and no numbers. What does the skill say to do before editing code?
evals.expected_output: The loop from SKILL.md: confirm the numbers come from a release build and check [profile.release] (build-config), take an end-to-end baseline, profile on realistic data to locate the hotspot instead of guessing, fix at the highest applicable leverage level (algorithm > allocations > layout/collections > parallelism > codegen > unsafe), then re-measure and keep or revert. A predicted speedup is a hypothesis, not a result.

assertions.text: Defines a leverage order with algorithm first
Puts unsafe last with measured justification

evals.prompt: My hand-rolled Instant::now() benchmark reports 0ns and my optimization shows no difference. Why, and what should I use instead?
evals.expected_output: Two stacked bugs: debug build (cargo run without --release) and dead-code elimination of the unused pure result. Fix with std::hint::black_box on both input and output plus a release build, then move to a real harness: criterion with --save-baseline/--baseline comparison, divan, iai-callgrind for CI-stable instruction counts, hyperfine for whole-binary A/B. Also lists traps: tiny inputs, warm-cache-only, thermal throttle, micro-bench vs end-to-end (Amdahl).

assertions.text: Names dead-code elimination as the 0ns cause
Prescribes black_box on input and output

evals.prompt: Which profiler or measurement tool do I pick for: CPU hotspots, allocation counts, cache misses, async runtime stalls, and whole-binary A/B?
evals.expected_output: The tool-by-question table: samply / cargo flamegraph (CPU sampling), perf record or Instruments deeper, dhat-rs or heaptrack (allocations), perf stat -d (cache/branch misses, IPC), tokio-console (async), hyperfine (whole binary), iai-callgrind (CI), cargo bloat / cargo llvm-lines (size). Plus debug = "line-tables-only" or a [profile.profiling] section so release stacks have symbols, and profiling on realistic prod-shaped data.

assertions.text: Covers perf stat for cache/IPC counters
Shows how to keep symbols in release builds

evals.prompt: My hot loop is dominated by a HashMap<String, u64>. What are the hasher options and their security trade-offs, and how do I avoid allocating a String per lookup?
evals.expected_output: SipHash is DoS-resistant but slow on short keys; foldhash/ahash are the seeded 2-3x general-purpose upgrade; rustc-hash (FxHash) is fastest but has zero flood resistance so only for provably internal keys. Entry API kills double lookups but needs an owned key; the std pattern is get_mut on the borrowed &str then insert only on miss; entry_ref is a hashbrown API, NOT stable std. Pre-size with with_capacity.

assertions.text: Names SipHash as the slow default
Offers foldhash/ahash as seeded fast options
States the DoS caveat for fxhash-style hashers
Corrects entry_ref as hashbrown, not std

evals.prompt: What release-profile and build-level wins can I take before changing any code?
evals.expected_output: lto (thin/fat), codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort" (with the catch_unwind semantics warning), strip, RUSTFLAGS -C target-cpu=native (portability caveat, x86-64-v3 middle ground), a global allocator swap (mimalloc/jemalloc) for alloc-heavy work, PGO via cargo-pgo once the workload is representative, plus pinned toolchain and lean dev debug info.

assertions.text: Sets lto in the release profile

evals.prompt: My axum service's p99 explodes under load and even cheap unrelated endpoints get slow. What's the diagnosis path and fix?
evals.expected_output: Signature of executor starvation: blocking or heavy CPU inside async fn parks a worker; cooperative scheduling means unrelated tasks queue behind it. Confirm with tokio-console (poll times should be micros). Fix: spawn_blocking wrapping the whole sequential chain in one hop, Semaphore to bound concurrent heavy work, dedicated pool for sustained CPU, regression greps for std::fs/::blocking/sync Mutex in async code.

assertions.text: Wraps the whole chain in one spawn_blocking
Bounds heavy concurrency with a Semaphore

evals.prompt: Iteration over a big Vec of enums is slow and perf stat shows heavy cache misses. What layout levers does the skill offer?
evals.expected_output: Check size_of (const assert against a cache line); an enum is as big as its largest variant so Box the fat variant (clippy::large_enum_variant); niche optimization makes Option<Box<T>> free; repr(Rust) already reorders fields; AoS to SoA flip when hot loops sweep few fields; indices into a flat Vec instead of Box/Rc pointer chasing; sequential iteration order for the prefetcher.

assertions.text: Replaces pointer chasing with flat Vec indices

evals.prompt: When is get_unchecked acceptable, and what should be tried before it?
evals.expected_output: Last resort only: first iterate instead of index, hoist a slice bound so LLVM proves ranges, use chunks_exact/slice patterns for vectorization; get_unchecked only with a benchmark showing the bounds check is the bottleneck plus a written safety argument. Verify vectorization with cargo-show-asm rather than assuming.

evals.prompt: Threads/rayon added but throughput barely moved. What does the skill point at?
evals.expected_output: Parallelize last (waste runs faster in parallel, Amdahl caps wins); per-item work must dwarf scheduling (~1us floor, with_min_len/par_chunks); contention ladder for Arc<Mutex> (shrink, shard, thread-local merge), RwLock/arc-swap for read-mostly, Relaxed atomics for counters, CachePadded for false sharing, and the busy-cores-vs-idle-cores differential to decide CPU-bound vs blocked.

assertions.text: States the per-item work floor for rayon
Gives the contention ladder for shared Mutex

evals.prompt: Should this hot inner-loop callback be Box<dyn Fn> or generic, and where do #[inline] attributes actually help?
evals.expected_output: Generic (impl Fn) in the hot core: direct calls inline and optimize through; dyn for cold/heterogeneous paths. Real dyn cost is lost inlining, not the indirect branch. Monomorphization bloat measured with cargo llvm-lines/cargo bloat, contained with the inner-dyn thin-wrapper trick. #[inline]: nothing within a crate, small non-generic cross-crate fns, never scatter inline(always) without a benchmark; #[cold]/inline(never) for slow paths.

assertions.text: Puts generics in the hot core, dyn in cold paths
Identifies lost inlining as the real dyn cost
Offers cold attribute for slow paths

evals.prompt: The profiler shows malloc/free wide in the flamegraph. What's the fix ladder for allocations?
evals.expected_output: Smell/fix table: clone-in-loop to borrowing, format! to write! into a reused String (itoa/ryu extreme), with_capacity, delete mid-pipeline collect, hoisted clear()+reuse buffers as the workhorse; then type-level: Box<str>/Arc<str>, SmallVec with its branch/size caveats, interning, arenas (bumpalo), serde borrow. Source fixes beat allocator swaps; don't contort lifetimes for cold-path clones.

assertions.text: Gives SmallVec caveats, not blanket advice
Cold-path clone is fine; hot-path clone is the target
